items.stem: What is machine code?
options: Binary instructions that the processor can execute directly
items.answer: Binary instructions that the processor can execute directly
items.markingKey: Machine code: binary opcodes and operands specific to the processor's instruction set.

items.stem: Describe what happens in each pass of a two-pass assembler.
items.answer: Pass 1: reads the program, removes comments, and builds the symbol table of labels and their addresses (and handles directives). Pass 2: uses the symbol table to replace labels with addresses and translates opcodes into machine code.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: pass 1 builds symbol table; 1 mark: forward references/labels recorded; 1 mark: pass 2 generates machine code with addresses replaced [3]

items.stem: Explain why a programmer might write part of a program in assembly language.
items.answer: For direct control of hardware/registers; for code that must be very fast or very small, e.g. a device driver or embedded system.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: hardware control; 1 mark: speed/memory efficiency [2]

items.stem: A programmer at Palm Grove Hotel in Lima has written a hardware control routine in assembly language; it contains a jump to a label that appears later in the code. (a) Explain why the program must be translated before it can be run. (b) Describe two features of the symbol table.
items.answer: (a) The processor can only execute machine code (binary); assembly mnemonics must be converted by an assembler. (b) Holds labels/symbolic names; their addresses; built in pass 1; used in pass 2.

items.stem: Explain one disadvantage of writing in assembly language rather than a high-level language.
items.answer: It is specific to one processor so not portable, and is harder and slower to write, read and debug.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: not portable/hard to write; 1 mark: explanation [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why a programmer might write part of a program in assembly language. (b) Describe what happens in each pass of a two-pass assembler.

items.stem: Mei is writing part of a device driver for Nova Telecom in assembly language. The program includes a JMP to a label defined later in the program. (a) Explain how a two-pass assembler deals with the forward reference. (b) Give two reasons for using assembly language for this task.
items.answer: (a) Pass 1 records the label address in the symbol table; pass 2 substitutes the address when generating machine code. (b) Direct access to registers/hardware; efficient (fast, small) code.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark pass 1; 1 mark pass 2 [2] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: A programmer at SkyLink Airways in Cairo has written a hardware control routine in assembly language; it contains a jump to a label that appears later in the code. (a) Explain why the program must be translated before it can be run. (b) Describe two features of the symbol table. (c) Explain the difference between an opcode and an operand.
items.answer: (a) The processor can only execute machine code (binary); assembly mnemonics must be converted by an assembler. (b) Holds labels/symbolic names; their addresses; built in pass 1; used in pass 2. (c) Opcode specifies the operation (and addressing mode); operand holds the data or address used.

items.stem: Which addressing mode is used by LDM #25?
items.answer: Immediate
items.markingKey: Immediate: the operand is the value itself.

items.stem: Explain why indexed addressing is useful when processing an array.
items.answer: The base address stays the same while the index register is incremented, so a loop can access consecutive elements with one instruction.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: base + IX; 1 mark: increment IX in loop to step through elements [2]

items.stem: Explain the benefit of relative addressing for code that may be loaded anywhere in memory.
items.answer: Jumps are given as offsets from the current instruction, so the code works whatever its start address (relocatable).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: offset from current address; 1 mark: relocatable [2]

items.stem: Explain how a loop is created in assembly language.
items.answer: A compare instruction tests a counter; a conditional jump (JPE/JPN) leaves the loop when the condition is met; an unconditional JMP at the end goes back to the start of the loop.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: counter changed each iteration; 1 mark: CMP and conditional jump; 1 mark: JMP back to start [3]

items.stem: What is the effect of a logical shift left of one place on an unsigned binary number (no bits lost)?
items.answer: It multiplies the value by 2

items.stem: Explain the difference between a logical shift and an arithmetic shift to the right.
items.answer: Logical shift right inserts 0 at the MSB end; arithmetic shift right copies the sign bit, so negative two's complement numbers stay negative (division by 2).

items.stem: A student at City Central Library is learning bit manipulation. Explain why an arithmetic shift is needed to divide a negative two's complement number by 2.
items.answer: A logical shift would put 0 into the sign bit, making the number positive; arithmetic shift copies the sign bit.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: The ACC contains 11010000. Give the contents of the ACC after OR #B11100011.

Address 200 contains 01010111. The program below is executed.
100  LDD 200
101  AND #B10101101
102  LSL #2
103  STO 201
104  LDD 200
105  XOR #B11111111
106  STO 202
107  END
(a) Give the binary value stored at 201. (b) Give the binary value stored at 202 and describe what instruction 105 does. (c) State the denary value at 201.
items.answer: (a) 00010100 (b) 10101000; inverts every bit (one's complement) (c) 20

items.stem: What does an assembler do?
options: Converts machine code into high-level code
Translates high-level code line by line as it runs
Translates assembly language into machine code
items.answer: Translates assembly language into machine code
items.markingKey: Assembler: one assembly instruction → one machine-code instruction (mostly).

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain one disadvantage of writing in assembly language rather than a high-level language. (b) Explain why a programmer might write part of a program in assembly language.
items.answer: (a) It is specific to one processor so not portable, and is harder and slower to write, read and debug. (b) For direct control of hardware/registers; for code that must be very fast or very small, e.g. a device driver or embedded system.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: not portable/hard to write; 1 mark: explanation [2] (b) 1 mark: hardware control; 1 mark: speed/memory efficiency [2]

items.stem:
A two-pass assembler translates the program below. Complete the symbol table (each label and its address) produced by pass 1, and identify one forward reference.
320  START: LDD STEP
321  CMP #0
322  JPE EXIT
323  DEC ACC
324  STO STEP
325  LDD VALUE
326  STO VALUE
327  JMP START
328  EXIT: END
329  STEP: 6
330  VALUE: 0
items.answer: START = 320, EXIT = 328, STEP = 329, VALUE = 330; forward reference: EXIT (or STEP) used before it is defined
items.markingKey: 1 mark per two correct entries (4 labels) [2]; forward reference identified [1] [3]

items.stem: A programmer at BlueWave Supermarkets in Mumbai has written a hardware control routine in assembly language; it contains a jump to a label that appears later in the code. (a) Explain why the program must be translated before it can be run. (b) Explain the difference between an opcode and an operand.
items.answer: (a) The processor can only execute machine code (binary); assembly mnemonics must be converted by an assembler. (b) Opcode specifies the operation (and addressing mode); operand holds the data or address used.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: In relative addressing, the address is calculated relative to what?
options: The address of the current instruction (or the PC)
items.answer: The address of the current instruction (or the PC)
items.markingKey: Relative: effective address = current instruction address + offset; allows relocatable code.

items.stem: State the instruction group for each of the instructions CMP #0 and CMI 200, and describe what each one does.
items.answer: CMP #0: compare; CMI 200: compare.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per correct group; 1 mark per description [4]

items.stem: State the instruction group for each of the instructions JPN 120 and JPE 150, and describe what each one does.
items.answer: JPN 120: conditional jump; JPE 150: conditional jump.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per correct group; 1 mark per description [4]

items.stem: The memory contains [150] = 39, [151] = 152, [152] = 7, [153] = 52, [154] = 26, [155] = 3 and the index register (IX) contains 1. What is the value in the ACC after the instruction LDM #154 is executed?
items.markingKey: immediate: the operand 154 itself is loaded.

items.stem: The memory contains [400] = 25, [401] = 403, [402] = 12, [403] = 12, [404] = 41, [405] = 49 and the index register (IX) contains 3. What is the value in the ACC after the instruction LDX 400 is executed?
items.markingKey: indexed: 400 + IX (3) = 403, contents 12.

items.stem:

51  LDX 400
52  ADD 402

items.answer: (a) 78 (b) 27 (c) LDR immediate, LDX indexed, LDI indirect

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) In a trace table for an assembly program, what is recorded? (b) Which instruction stops execution of a program?
items.answer: (a) The values in registers and memory locations after each instruction (b) END
items.markingKey: (a) A trace table follows the changes to ACC, IX, memory and output as each instruction runs. (b) END returns control to the operating system.

items.stem: A student at Riverside Medical Centre is tracing an assembly language loop. Explain how a trace table shows that a loop has finished.
items.answer: The counter reaches the exit value, the conditional jump is taken and the END instruction is reached.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem:
Memory contains [300] = 2, [301] = 2, [302] = 4. Trace the program below and state the final value stored at address 301 and at address 300.
200  LDD 300
201  CMP #0
202  JPE 210
203  DEC ACC
204  STO 300
205  LDD 301
206  ADD 302
207  STO 301
208  JMP 200
210  END
items.markingKey: The loop runs 2 times, adding [302] = 4 each time: 2 + 2 × 4 = 10; [300] counts down to 0 [2]

items.stem:
Memory contains [400] = 37, [401] = 32, [402] = 7, [403] = 9, [404] = 22, [500] = 0. The program below is executed.
100  LDR #0
101  LDX 400
102  CMP #32
103  JPE 110
104  INC IX
105  LDD 500
106  INC ACC
107  STO 500
108  CMP #5
109  JPN 101
110  END
(a) State the purpose of the program. (b) Give the final values of IX and of the contents of address 500. (c) Explain what the final value of IX tells the user.
items.answer: (a) Linear search of the 5 values at 400–404 for 32 (b) IX = 1, [500] = 1 (c) 32 was found at address 401; IX = 1 is its offset from address 400
items.markingKey: (a) searches for 32 [1] (b) IX = 1 [1]; [500] = 1 [1] (c) correct interpretation [2]

items.stem: A student at Orbit Games Studio is learning bit manipulation. Explain why a logical shift left by 1 place multiplies an unsigned number by 2.
items.answer: Every bit moves to the next higher place value (twice as large), with 0 entering at the right, provided no 1 is lost from the left.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: A student at SwiftCar Rentals is learning bit manipulation. Explain the difference between using OR and XOR with the same mask.
items.answer: OR always sets the masked bits to 1; XOR flips them, setting 0s to 1 and 1s to 0.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]
